title: The history of cheese
tagline: Seven thousand years from clay sieves on a Polish plain to enzymes brewed in steel tanks.
intro: Early farmers found that sour or curdled milk, drained of its whey, kept for longer and was easier on the stomach. Greeks and Romans wrote down how to use rennet, press and salt. Medieval monks and mountain villages shaped the cheeses we still name. Then factories, microscopes and pasteurisation made cheese an industry, India learned to make it from buffalo milk, and the enzyme that starts it all moved from calf stomachs to fermentation tanks.

eras.name: Herders and sieves
eras.summary: Early farmers cannot digest fresh milk well. Turning it into curd and cheese removes most of the lactose and lets milk be stored and carried.

eras.name: Rennet, presses and monasteries
eras.summary: Greek and Roman writers describe rennet, moulds, pressing and salting. In the Middle Ages monasteries and mountain villages give Europe many of its named cheeses.

eras.name: Named cheeses travel
eras.summary: Cheeses pick up names, rules and reputations, and cheesemaking travels with traders and missionaries as far as Bengal.

eras.name: Factories and microbes
eras.summary: Pooled milk, standard rennet, pure cultures and pasteurisation turn a farmhouse craft into an industry, and processed cheese is invented.

eras.name: Biotech, labels and old pots
eras.summary: India starts making cheese from buffalo milk, rennet moves from calves to fermentation tanks, names get legal protection, and chemistry reads cheese in ancient pottery.

events.title: Clay sieves strain the first known curds
events.who: Early farmers of the Linear Pottery culture
events.text: Farmers in Kuyavia, in what is now Poland, made pots full of small holes about 7,000 years ago. In 2012 chemists found milk fat soaked into the clay, which shows the pots were used to strain curd from whey. It is the earliest direct evidence of cheesemaking.
events.why: Cheese let people who could not digest fresh milk keep and eat it, because most of the lactose drains away in the whey.

events.title: Fermented dairy on the Dalmatian coast
events.text: Fat residues in pottery from two villages on the Dalmatian coast point to fermented dairy products, soft cheeses and yoghurts, about 7,200 years ago. Plain milk residues at the same sites are some 500 years older still.
events.why: It shows cheesemaking beside the Mediterranean at about the same time as in northern Europe.

events.title: Cheese in the account books of Ur
events.text: Clay tablets from the Third Dynasty of Ur record deliveries of cheese alongside butter and milk. They are among the oldest written mentions of cheese.
events.why: Cheese was already an everyday, counted and traded food.

events.title: The oldest cheese that still exists
events.text: Lumps of cheese were laid on the necks and chests of people buried in the desert about 3,600 years ago. In 2024 scientists read DNA from them and found it was kefir cheese, made with bacteria and yeasts like those in kefir grains today.
events.why: It is the oldest preserved cheese known, and it carries the oldest known cheese microbes.

events.title: A jar of cheese in an Egyptian tomb
events.who: Buried with Ptahmes, mayor of Memphis
events.text: A broken jar in the tomb of Ptahmes held a whitish mass. In 2018 chemists showed it was a solid cheese made from cow milk mixed with sheep or goat milk. It is about 3,200 years old.
events.why: It is the oldest solid cheese found in Egypt, identified by its proteins.

events.title: A giant makes cheese in the Odyssey
events.text: In the Odyssey, the Cyclops Polyphemus milks his sheep and goats, curdles half the milk and sets the curd in woven baskets to drain. The scene is one of the oldest descriptions of cheesemaking in literature.
events.why: It shows the same steps as today: curdle, drain, shape.

events.title: A Roman writes down the recipe
events.text: In his farming book De Re Rustica, Columella describes clotting milk with rennet from a lamb or kid, pressing the curd under weights, salting it and hardening it. About a decade later Pliny the Elder lists the cheeses Romans liked best.
events.why: Rennet, pressing, salting and ageing were all in use by Roman times.

events.title: Monks make Maroilles
events.who: A monk of the Abbey of Maroilles (traditional account)
events.text: Maroilles, a soft cheese with a washed orange rind, is often said to have first been made in 962 by a monk at the Abbey of Maroilles. The date rests on tradition, but monasteries really were centres of cheesemaking in medieval Europe.
events.why: Monasteries had cellars, time and written rules, which suited the slow work of ripening.

events.title: A king buys five tonnes of Cheddar
events.text: The royal accounts, called the Pipe Rolls, record that King Henry II bought 10,240 pounds of Cheddar cheese at a farthing a pound.
events.why: It is the earliest record of Cheddar, now one of the most made cheeses in the world.

events.title: Parmesan appears in writing
events.where: Parma and Reggio Emilia region, Italy
events.text: The earliest written record of Parmesan dates from 1254. By 1348 Boccaccio could joke in the Decameron about a mountain made of grated Parmesan.
events.why: A hard, long-keeping cheese could be traded across a continent.

events.title: Roquefort gets a royal monopoly
events.text: King Charles VI gave the people of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon the sole right to ripen the blue ewe-milk cheese in their limestone caves.
events.why: It is an early case of the law tying a cheese's name to one place.

events.title: The word mozzarella is printed
events.text: The papal cook Bartolomeo Scappi lists fresh mozzarella in his cookbook, the first time the word appears in print. Water buffalo, which probably reached Italy from Asia centuries earlier, gave the rich milk.
events.why: Stretched-curd cheese from buffalo milk became one of the world's favourites.

events.title: Bandel cheese in Bengal
events.who: Portuguese settlers and their Mog (Burmese) cooks
events.text: At the Portuguese settlement of Bandel on the Hooghly river, milk was curdled with lemon juice, drained in small baskets, salted and often smoked. The exact date is not recorded. A handful of families in West Bengal still make it.
events.why: It is one of the few cheeses born in India, and a cousin of the chhena behind Bengal's sweets.

events.title: Marie Harel and Camembert
events.text: Camembert is said to have first been made in 1791 by Marie Harel, a farmer in Normandy. Historians think the cheese we know owes more to late nineteenth-century dairies, and to the round wooden box invented in 1890 that let it travel.
events.why: The story made a soft, white-moulded cheese a symbol of France.

events.title: The first valley cheese dairy
events.text: Until then Swiss cheese was made in summer on the high Alpine pastures. In 1815 a dairy was built on an estate in the valley village of Kiesen, taking milk from farms around it all year round.
events.why: Many small farms sharing one dairy is the idea behind every cheese factory and cooperative.

events.title: The first American cheese factory
events.text: Jesse Williams, a farmer known for good cheese, began buying milk from his neighbours and making it all into cheese in one building. The factory was soon turning out well over 25,000 pounds a year, and the idea spread quickly across New York State.
events.why: Cheese moved from the farmhouse kitchen to the factory.

events.title: Cheddar by the thermometer
events.text: Joseph Harding and his family worked out a fixed method for Cheddar: clean dairies, measured temperatures, a set order of steps and a revolving cutter for the curd. They taught it in Scotland, and visitors carried it to America and Australia.
events.why: A recipe ruled by measurement could be repeated anywhere.

events.title: Pasteur's gentle heating
events.text: Louis Pasteur showed that warming wine to about 50 to 60 °C killed the microbes that spoiled it. In 1886 Franz von Soxhlet proposed doing the same to milk. Dairies now pasteurise most cheese milk at about 72 °C for 15 seconds.
events.why: Safe milk that still clots made large-scale cheesemaking dependable.

events.title: Rennet in a bottle
events.text: The Danish chemist Christian Hansen set up a laboratory to make a clean rennet extract of known strength from calf stomachs. Cheesemakers no longer had to soak dried stomachs themselves. By 1878 the firm was working in the United States.
events.why: A measured dose of rennet gives the same clotting time every day.

events.title: The microbes get names
events.who: Eduard von Freudenreich, Sigurd Orla-Jensen and Charles Thom
events.text: In Switzerland, von Freudenreich and Orla-Jensen showed that propionic acid bacteria in Emmental turn lactate into propionic acid, acetic acid and carbon dioxide, the gas that blows the holes. The same year the American Charles Thom described the moulds Penicillium camemberti and Penicillium roqueforti.
events.why: Once the microbes were known they could be grown as pure cultures and added on purpose.

events.title: Processed cheese is invented
events.text: Looking for a cheese that would keep in warm countries, Gerber and Stettler melted Emmentaler with sodium citrate. The salt bound the calcium, and the melted cheese stayed smooth instead of turning oily.
events.why: Emulsifying salts are still what make processed cheese melt evenly.

events.title: Kraft patents cheese that keeps
events.text: James L. Kraft received US patent 1,186,524 for heating and stirring cheese so that it could be sealed in tins and keep without spoiling. Tinned cheese fed armies in the First World War.
events.why: Cheese became a packaged, branded food sold far from any dairy.

events.title: Roquefort is the first protected name
events.text: Roquefort became the first cheese with a French appellation d'origine, a law saying what it must be made from and where it must be ripened.
events.why: Later systems for protecting food names copied this model.

events.title: A Swiss priest makes cheese in Kalimpong
events.text: A Swiss Jesuit, Father André Butty, set up the Swiss Welfare Dairy in the hill town of Kalimpong in the 1950s to support a mission orphanage, and began making a Gouda-style wheel. The dairy closed around 1990, but local families still make Kalimpong cheese.
events.why: It became one of India's best-known ripened cheeses.

events.title: Amul makes cheese from buffalo milk
events.who: Kaira District Co-operative Milk Producers' Union (Amul)
events.text: Most Indian milk came from buffaloes, and experts abroad doubted it could be made into Cheddar-style cheese. The farmers' cooperative at Anand added a cheese plant in the late 1950s and sold processed cheese under the Amul name, reported as the first large-scale cheese from buffalo milk. Accounts give 1958 or 1959.
events.why: It showed that cheese could be made at scale from the milk India actually had.

events.title: A world standard for cheese
events.text: The Codex General Standard for Cheese set out what may be called cheese and how to describe it as soft, firm, hard or extra hard by its moisture. National rules, including India's, build on it.
events.why: Shared definitions let cheese be traded and labelled the same way across borders.

events.title: Rennet from a fermentation tank
events.who: US Food and Drug Administration; Pfizer
events.text: Calf rennet was running short. Scientists put the calf's chymosin gene into microbes, which then made the same enzyme in a tank. In 1990 the FDA accepted it as safe, the first food ingredient made by genetic engineering to be approved. It now clots most of the world's cheese.
events.why: Cheese no longer depends on calf stomachs, which matters to vegetarians and in India.

events.title: Europe protects cheese names
events.text: A European law of 1992 created protected designations of origin for foods. Roquefort, Parmigiano Reggiano, feta and Stilton may now carry their names only if made in their home region by the set method.
events.why: A name on a cheese became a legal promise about place and method.

events.title: Hay dust seeds the holes
events.text: Swiss scientists reported that the eyes in Emmental start on microscopic specks of hay in the milk, where the carbon dioxide can gather into a bubble. Cleaner modern milking had been giving cheeses with fewer and smaller holes.
events.why: It explained why the holes had been shrinking for years.

events.title: GI tags for yak churpi and kaladi
events.text: Arunachal Pradesh Yak Churpi, made by Brokpa herders from the milk of the Arunachali yak, received a geographical indication tag. So did Udhampur's kaladi (kalari), the stretched, pan-seared cheese of Jammu.
events.why: India's own cheeses gained the same kind of name protection as Roquefort.

people.name: Columella
people.note: His farming manual gives one of the first full recipes for rennet cheese.

people.name: Marie Harel
people.note: Credited by tradition with the first Camembert in 1791.

people.name: Jesse Williams
people.note: Pooled his neighbours' milk in 1851 and started the cheese factory system.

people.name: Joseph Harding
people.note: Called the father of Cheddar for his measured, hygienic method.

people.name: Louis Pasteur
people.note: Showed that gentle heat stops microbes spoiling food and drink.

people.name: Christian D. A. Hansen
people.note: Made the first standard rennet extract and founded the firm Chr. Hansen in 1874.

people.name: Sigurd Orla-Jensen
people.note: Worked out, with Eduard von Freudenreich, how propionic bacteria make the holes in Emmental.

people.name: Charles Thom
people.note: Described and named the moulds of Camembert and Roquefort in 1906.

people.name: Walter Gerber
people.note: Invented processed cheese with Fritz Stettler in 1911.

people.name: James L. Kraft
people.note: Patented a way to make cheese keep in tins in 1916.

people.name: Verghese Kurien
people.note: Led the Anand cooperative that made cheese and milk powder from buffalo milk.

people.note: Started the Swiss Welfare Dairy and Kalimpong cheese in the 1950s.

facts: It takes about 10 litres of cow milk to make 1 kg of hard cheese. About nine-tenths of the milk leaves as whey.
The holes in Emmental are bubbles of carbon dioxide made by bacteria, and each bubble starts on a speck of hay dust.
The enzyme in rennet cuts just one bond in one milk protein, between amino acids 105 and 106 of kappa-casein.
A wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano weighs about 38 kg, floats in brine for 20 to 25 days and is aged for at least a year.
Long-aged cheeses such as Parmesan and mature Cheddar contain almost no lactose, because bacteria use it up in the first weeks.
